title: Reason through authority conscience and a disputed practice

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Conscience can justify examining or refusing a demand while leaving legitimate coordination and another person’s rights intact. Authority has a scope; disagreement with one demand does not erase every boundary.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: The supplied reading circle permits silent observation, ends at 11:00 and prohibits recording other participants. A teacher asks all visitors to say gratitude words. Jo cannot honestly affirm them but is willing to remain quiet and leave on time. The coordinator accepts private procedure questions and can correct the teacher’s request.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Compare the teacher’s unity reason with truthful silence, then identify which other boundaries Jo must still respect. Draft a proportionate private clarification.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A visitor says conscience requires publicly streaming a private discussion despite the participants’ no-recording boundary. Is dissent sufficient authority?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Ask the coordinator to preserve the written observation route or choose to leave. Jo’s conscience does not authorize recording participants or extending the room booking. Later fiction: coordinator confirms silence is allowed and closes on time; no wider authority judgment follows. Partial: oppose compulsion without acknowledging ordinary rules. Incorrect: treat every unwanted restriction as an assault on conscience.
criteria: Dissent does not erase other rights
The response is proportionate and honest

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. The asserted belief does not create consent to expose others. Use a permitted account or appropriate concern process while respecting privacy and safety.
